SDR16C5.summary: The epithelial signal warrants an organoid test, but the case for inhibition depends on what silencing does to the lining.

reasons.text: The increase persists within epithelial cells across cohorts. The predicted pocket offers a possible drug route, while the absence of functional evidence leaves the therapeutic direction open.

CYP4X1.summary: I would test CYP4X1 silencing only with crypt regrowth as an explicit outcome.

reasons.text: Expression rises in regenerating crypt cells, so impaired regrowth would count against inhibition even if chemokine release fell. The dossier supports investigating a small molecule and reports no extracellular region.

CPXM1.summary: I would back CPXM1 blockade in primary UC fibroblasts as a first-in-class experiment.

reasons.text: The secreted protein offers a direct intervention, and expression rises within fibroblast subsets despite the contribution from cell composition. The proposed neutrophil-attraction assay can test a consequence of blockade.

CHRDL2.summary: CHRDL2 is accessible to an antibody, but a fibroblast-only result would leave its role in intact mucosa unresolved.

reasons.text: Only 28% of the bulk rise survives adjustment, and the spatial signal points to smooth muscle. A negative fibroblast experiment would therefore leave uncertainty about the relevant source.

SERPINB5.summary: SERPINB5 is my first choice for epithelial silencing because human tissue and both mouse perturbations support testing the same direction.

reasons.text: The paired-biopsy increase and replicated epithelial localization make the organoid experiment interpretable. The unresolved cancer association limits what short-term protection could establish about prolonged treatment.

CXCL1.summary: I would back CXCL1 neutralisation to test recruitment, with a narrower interpretation than therapeutic benefit.

reasons.text: The proposed co-culture directly tests the inferred fibroblast–neutrophil circuit. A fall in migration would support that mechanism, while leaving the effect on mucosal injury open.

CHI3L1.summary: I would test CHI3L1 blockade because the parallel fibroblast and epithelial experiments can resolve a consequential disagreement.

reasons.text: Antibody treatment and gene deletion gave opposite colitis outcomes. An epithelial injury signal would weigh against advancing blockade even if fibroblast inflammatory readouts improved.

REG1B.summary: I would back the paired silencing and protein-addition experiment while leaving the therapeutic direction open.

reasons.text: The consistent epithelial source makes organoids appropriate. The biomarker evidence and link to regeneration leave open whether the rise contributes to injury or supports recovery.

INHBA.summary: I would test activin-pathway inhibition in UC explants, with limited confidence that a response establishes INHBA as the target.

reasons.text: The follistatin result supports a pathway-level hypothesis. Inconsistent cellular attribution and strong loss constraint limit the inference from a positive fibroblast or macrophage result.

CFB.summary: I would deprioritise CFB inhibition because its strongest directional warning concerns loss of the very function the drug would block.

reasons.text: The human loss-of-function signal comes from perianal Crohn’s disease, so its relevance to UC remains uncertain. Epithelial induction and higher protein alone offer insufficient justification to prioritise iptacopan given the deficiency phenotype.

LY96.summary: I would back eritoran in UC explants if recovery is treated as a decisive outcome.

reasons.text: Early anti-inflammatory effects could coexist with impaired healing, as the dossier describes for complex blockade. The proposed two-phase readout addresses this risk more directly than the response associations.

SELP.summary: I would deprioritise SELP even though the proposed flow assay is well matched to P-selectin biology.

reasons.text: A flow assay could establish an effect on adhesion. The negative antibody result in experimental colitis and similar associations in both treatment arms weaken the case for spending a year on therapeutic blockade.

TUFM.summary: I would back a cell-restricted TUFM genetic experiment on the strength of the colocalising signal, while deferring drug development.

reasons.text: Replication gives the single-instrument result weight. The unresolved effector cell and ubiquitous mitochondrial expression make systemic inhibition a poor inference from that result.

CEBPB.summary: I would test CEBPB silencing in risk-allele carriers as a cell-specific genetic hypothesis.

reasons.text: The dendritic-cell prediction and active regulon justify the experiment, but most measured RNA comes from other myeloid cells and Mendelian randomisation gives no concordant support for inhibition.

FIGNL1.summary: I would deprioritise FIGNL1 as a therapeutic target while retaining the NK-cell allele-specific expression question.

reasons.text: Fine mapping and a matching lineage justify checking expression. Neither the biopsy data nor Mendelian randomisation independently supports inhibition, and filling a shortlist slot adds no biological evidence.

CFAP90.summary: I would defer CFAP90 inhibition until the proposed goblet-cell expression effect is demonstrated.

reasons.text: The prediction spans several cell types, and neither biopsy expression nor Mendelian randomisation corroborates the proposed direction. Confirming the expression effect is a narrower objective than developing a UC treatment.
